title: "Ask them, if they can speak"
hookLine: the people accuse him, and he tells them to ask the idols, and they fall silent (21:62–65)

lines: WHO DID THIS TO OUR GODS?
BRING HIM OUT, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.
cards: The festival is over, and the town comes home. Someone walks into the temple and stops dead. Pieces everywhere: heads on the floor, arms snapped off.
And in the middle of the wreckage, the biggest idol, untouched, standing tall. Who did this to our gods? Word goes around about a young man who's been talking about them.
His name is Ibrahim. Bring him out, they say, in front of everyone. They ask him straight out, and his answer turns the question around.

teach.b: Surah twenty-one. They ask: Ibrahim, was it you who did this to our gods? He points at the big one.

teach.h: QUESTION THEM, IF THEY CAN SPEAK.
teach.b: In Pickthall's words: “But this, their chief hath done it. So question them, if they can speak.” And the crowd goes quiet.
The Qur'an says they turned to one another, and to themselves, and said: surely it's you who are the wrongdoers.

teach.h: A MOMENT OF HONESTY, THEN BACK.
teach.b: A real moment of honesty. For one breath, the whole town sees it: statues that can't say who broke them can't hear a prayer either. Then the next verse says, literally, that they were turned back onto their heads.
The old thinking came flooding back, and they said to him: “Well thou knowest that these speak not.” Listen to what they just admitted.
Ibrahim asks: then do you worship, instead of God, what can neither help you nor harm you? So was his answer, their chief did it, a lie?
A hadith in Bukhari counts it among three times Ibrahim said something not literally true, and says two of them, this one included, were for God's sake.
Scholars explain it as a pointed kind of irony, said so the listeners would work out for themselves that it couldn't be true.
The moment you say it can't speak, you've answered your own question. Ibrahim didn't win an argument. He let them hear themselves say it.

how: Muslims read Ibrahim's questioning of the idols as a model of patient reasoning, and teachers use his words to invite people to think honestly about what they rely on.

games.q: you're Ibrahim, in front of the whole town. they ask: was it you who did this to our gods? what do you say?
o: yes, and your gods are nothing.
this big one did it. ask them, if they can speak.
games.why: "But this, their chief hath done it. So question them, if they can speak." and they had to say it themselves: they cannot speak.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you give power to that has none: a number on a scale, a like count, an old voice from school. Ask it Ibrahim's question, can you help me, or harm me, really?
Listen to the silence, and if you pray, turn toward the One who hears.

wordCard.voice: Ask them. Ibrahim's answer to the crowd: question the idols, if they can speak. And the town admits they cannot.
